questions.q: Why do ML artifacts typically get split across object storage, a registry backing store, and a container registry instead of using one system for everything?
options: Because it is required by law
Each system is optimized for a different shape of artifact, and mixing them up throws away the tooling each is actually built for
Because object storage cannot store any binary files
Because container registries are being phased out
questions.explain: Object storage, registry metadata stores, and container registries each specialize in a different kind of artifact (blobs, structured metadata, layered images respectively).

questions.q: In the MLflow server example, what is stored in the Postgres database versus the S3 bucket?
options: Everything is stored only in Postgres
Run parameters, metrics, and tags go to Postgres, while logged model/artifact bytes go to the S3 artifact root
Everything is stored only in S3
S3 stores the metadata and Postgres stores the model binaries
questions.explain: MLflow's backend-store-uri (database) holds metadata like params and tags, while default-artifact-root (object storage) holds the actual artifact bytes.

questions.q: What does the example S3 lifecycle rule do to objects under the `training-logs/` prefix?
options: It immediately deletes them on creation
It transitions them to Glacier storage after 30 days and deletes them after 365 days
It duplicates them to a second region
It converts them to a different file format
questions.explain: The rule moves aging training logs to cheaper cold storage after 30 days and expires them entirely after a year.

questions.q: According to the lesson, which artifacts should generally be kept long-term rather than expired aggressively?
options: Intermediate training logs from failed hyperparameter sweeps
Deployed/recently-superseded model versions and reproducibility manifests for anything that was ever in production
Scratch datasets used only for a single failed experiment
Every artifact regardless of type or purpose
questions.explain: Deployed models and their reproducibility manifests are small and audit-critical, making them worth retaining even though other artifacts can be expired.

questions.q: How does the lesson say retention policy and auditability requirements should be reconciled?
options: By deleting everything after a fixed 90-day window regardless of purpose
Through tiering: aggressively expiring cheap, regenerable artifacts while keeping small, audit-critical artifacts for the full regulatory window
By keeping every single artifact forever with no policy at all
Auditability requirements should simply be ignored in favor of cost savings
questions.explain: Tiering resolves the tension: low-value, bulky artifacts are expired quickly, while small, audit-critical ones are retained long-term since they cost little to keep.
